---
title: "Getting started"
---

## Imports

phplyr's table functions and helpers are namespaced functions. Import the ones a file
uses with `use function`:

```php
use Phibble\DataFrame;
use function Phplyr\{phplyr, filter, mutate, group_by, summarise, arrange, desc, n, mean};
```

A method chain only needs `phplyr()` and the helpers it uses, such as `n`,
`mean`, and `desc`. The table functions are its methods.

Three phplyr functions share names with PHP built-ins: `count`, `min`, and
`max`. In a file that imports them, a bare `count($array)` calls phplyr's
`count()`. Write `\count()`, `\min()`, and `\max()` for the built-ins.

## Loading data

phibble reads CSV files, PDO queries, and query builders, and builds frames from
PHP arrays:

```php
$schools = DataFrame::fromCsv('schools.csv');
$rows = DataFrame::fromRows([['id' => 1, 'x' => 2.5], ['id' => 2, 'x' => null]]);
$cols = DataFrame::fromColumns(['id' => [1, 2], 'x' => [2.5, null]]);
```

`null` is NA. DataFrames are immutable, and every function returns a new frame.
`echo $frame` prints the first rows in tibble's format.

## Chaining functions

A function such as `filter(...)` returns a closure that takes a table. phplyr runs
a sequence of them in three ways, and all three give the same result.

::: {.panel-tabset group="syntax"}

## Method chain (PHP 8.3+)

`phplyr($t)` starts a chain. Each method runs the phplyr function of that name
with the same arguments, and `get()` returns the table:

```php
$out = phplyr($schools)
    ->filter(fn ($r) => $r->score > 80)
    ->arrange(desc('score'))
    ->get();
```

`echo` prints a chain's table directly. A function whose result isn't a table,
such as `pull()`, `n_groups()`, or `lm()`, returns that result and ends the
chain. `->pipe($closure)` applies a closure of your own and continues.

## Pipe (PHP 8.5)

The pipe operator calls each closure with the value on its left:

```php
$out = $schools
    |> filter(fn ($r) => $r->score > 80)
    |> arrange(desc('score'));
```

:::

`pipe()` applies the closures in order and works on every PHP version:

```php
$out = pipe($schools, filter(fn ($r) => $r->score > 80), arrange(desc('score')));
// is the same as
$out = arrange(desc('score'))(filter(fn ($r) => $r->score > 80)($schools));
```

The rest of this guide shows each example both as a method chain and with
`|>`. The two are interchangeable.

Columns are named with strings: write `'score'` where dplyr takes a bare
`score`.

## Row closures and vector helpers

phplyr accepts two kinds of expressions.

A **row closure** is an ordinary PHP closure. It receives the row as a
`Phibble\Row` (read columns as `$r->score` or `$r['score']`) and, as a second
argument, the table of the row's group:

```php
mutate(gap: fn ($r) => $r->score - $r->prior_score)
filter(fn ($r, $group) => $r->score > mean('score')($group))
```

A **vector helper** is one of phplyr's functions, such as `lag('x')`,
`cumsum('x')`, `min_rank('x')`, or `mean('x')`. It is evaluated once per group
on whole columns, with dplyr's semantics. A summary helper used in `mutate()`
returns one value per group, which is recycled to every row of the group:

{{< include examples/_grouping.md >}}

Vector helpers take a column name as their first argument. That argument can
also be `col('x')`, another helper, or a row closure. Later arguments are
values, so a string there is a literal. Wrap it in `col()` to refer to a
column.

A third form, `col('x')->mul(2)`, builds an inspectable expression. Expressions
behave like the helpers in memory, and they let the same pipeline run as SQL on
a database table. See [Databases and expressions](reference/databases.qmd).

## Named arguments and options

Functions that create columns name them with PHP named arguments:
`mutate(total: ...)`, `summarise(n: n())`. dplyr's dot-prefixed options are
written with a leading underscore, because PHP named arguments cannot start with
a dot: `_by`, `_keep`, `_before`, `_after`, `_groups`, `_keep_all`, and
`_by_group`.

PHP does not allow positional arguments after named ones. Put `across()` and
other positional arguments first: `summarise(across(...), n: n())`.

## Printing and inspecting

`echo` prints a frame. `glimpse()` prints one line per column and passes the
table through, so it can sit inside a pipeline. `pull('x')` returns a column as
a PHP list, and `$frame->toRows()` returns all rows as arrays.
